Vignette: Gerald

Gerald is a 61-year-old married man who has driven city buses for the past twenty-two years. He is broad-shouldered and deliberate in the way he moves, someone who gives the impression of having always been steady, the kind of man others naturally lean on. That steadiness is something he works hard to maintain now, though it costs him considerably more than it once did.

Eleven years ago, Gerald traveled to Central America to visit his younger brother, who had been doing missionary work there for several years. On his third day in the country, Gerald was taken at gunpoint by members of a local paramilitary faction who had mistaken him for someone connected to a rival organization. He was held for nine days in a concrete room with no natural light. During that time he was beaten repeatedly, deprived of sleep through noise and cold water, and subjected to mock executions on at least three separate occasions - men pressing a gun to his temple, counting down, and pulling the trigger on an empty chamber. He was eventually released after his brother made contact with local authorities and a ransom was quietly arranged. Gerald flew home alone, wearing borrowed clothes, and told almost no one what had actually happened.

For the first two years he functioned, more or less. He returned to his route, drove his bus, came home to his wife, Marlene. He told himself he was fine. He told himself he was lucky. But he stopped sleeping through the night almost immediately after returning home. He would wake at two or three in the morning with his heart hammering, certain - absolutely certain - that someone was in the room. He began checking the locks four and five times before bed. He stopped answering the door unless he was expecting someone.

The bus became its own complicated terrain. Gerald sits in an enclosed cab, separated from passengers by a plexiglass partition, and for a long time that felt like protection. But certain sounds - a sudden shout from the back of the bus, a door slamming at a stop, even the particular pitch of a bus's air brakes - can send him somewhere else entirely. His hands tighten on the wheel. His vision narrows. He is back in that concrete room, counting his own breaths, waiting. He has learned to manage these moments without passengers noticing, which is a source of both pride and exhaustion.

Gerald does not talk about what happened, not with Marlene, not with his adult children, not with the few friends he still sees. He describes himself as a private person and believes, genuinely, that talking about it would only spread the damage to people he loves. Marlene knows something is wrong. She has known for years. She describes a husband who flinches at small things, who has become unreachable in the evenings, who sometimes sits at the kitchen table long after dinner staring at nothing she can identify. Their intimacy has narrowed considerably. Gerald feels the distance and does not know how to close it without opening a door he is afraid to open.

He carries a persistent sense that the world is fundamentally unsafe in a way it was not before - not as an abstract belief but as a bodily fact, something he feels in his chest when he is in an unfamiliar neighborhood or when a passenger boards his bus wearing a hood pulled low. He is irritable in ways he did not used to be, short with Marlene over small things, and afterward ashamed of himself. He drinks two or three whiskeys most evenings, which he describes as helping him wind down, though he acknowledges it has become less optional over time.

What brought Gerald in was not a crisis but an accumulation - a moment last spring when a teenager on his bus pulled out a toy gun as a joke and Gerald had to pull the bus to the curb, hands shaking, unable to continue his route. He sat there for eleven minutes before he could drive again. He has not told his supervisor what happened. He is not sure, anymore, how much longer he can hold it all in place.
